Senses.Explanation: “Hammer out the phoenix's five-colored marrow” is an extravagant smithing image for forceful handling that brings out something rare and inward. Cuiyan Zhe says Ciming's tongs and hammer brought out the phoenix's five-colored marrow. Lianyue Daozheng independently reuses the image while describing forceful public activity. Guxue, Xiangya, Huijue and Yuanan each actively deploy the phoenix-marrow image in distinct current teachings rather than merely copying the old Cuiyan line.

Senses.Explanation: 敲甎 is to knock or hammer bricks, and 打瓦 is to strike or work tiles. Ying’an, Huanji, and Mi’an use the building noise disparagingly; Ying’an condemns making disorder with old cases, Huanji says verse-workers miss Xuedou’s lifeline, and Mi’an condemns both old worthies before separately criticizing Langye. Baofu and Guanghui use the phrase as terse answers, while Huqiu treats it as an activity his audience should eventually outgrow; these turns prevent a single abstract replacement from exhausting the phrase.

Senses.Explanation: 敲甎打瓦 can literally mean “knock bricks and set tiles,” doing masonry work. Liaotang’s poem is headed “Constructing Three Stupas” and follows the phrase with 見功成, “see the work completed,” which makes literal masonry locally defensible.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Strike empty space and it sounds; strike wood and it makes no sound
AlternateTargets: Knock on emptiness and hear it ring; strike wood and hear nothing
SearchAliases: strike empty space sounds strike wood no sound
Senses.Note: The paradox reverses ordinary expectations about sound and material. Masters speak it while striking, questioning, or displaying a staff, so the pair directs attention to the present act rather than asserting a rule of physics.

Senses.Explanation: "Strike empty space and it sounds; strike wood and it makes no sound" reverses what the ear expects. In these records masters put the pair beside an action or a question, making the listener test the expectation in the present turn. Fushi strikes the air with a firebrand as he utters the pair. Baochi uses the pair in a hall address; Tianran speaks it with a strike and gesture. Dounan applies it to his staff teaching.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB390.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chulin of Beijing. Chulin Shangrui takes his staff and knocks at empty space, asking who knows the tune of the sound he is making. He then strikes the wooden seat but says that striking wood makes no sound and that cocking an ear is wasted effort. This reversal throws the person of no rank into confusion, and Chulin asks how the assembly will act as that person's master. If it cannot, he says that he has lost today. The headword belongs to Chulin's present enacted test; it does not report an acoustic experiment proving that empty space rings or wood is silent.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1343.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baojue Zuxin (Huanglong Four Houses Record, No. 2). Huitang Zuxin opens a hall address by asking who knows the tune when empty space is struck, then says that striking things produces no sound and listening attentively is futile. He continues that this is not an object immediately before the eyes and warns against producing further thoughts about it. His elephant-king, moon-in-water and wind-and-cloud images lead to a demand to sweep away previous accomplishments, actions, understanding and nonunderstanding alike. He closes by preferring a return to the mountains and one long cry into the mist. The listener sought is tested by this whole demand, rather than identified simply by possessing good hearing or a verbal explanation of the opening question.

Senses.Explanation: Strike empty space and it resounds; strike wood and there is no sound. A reversal of expected sound that tests habitual sense-making. Current deployments include Ruibai Mingxue in J26nB188, Buhui Fatong in J32nB276, Liangting Jingting in J33nB294, Shenfeng Xian in J34nB298, and Yikui Yuankui in J37nB388. The full paired image remains the lexical unit. The acoustic reversal is a Chan image, not a physical claim about sound.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names the bright sun in the open sky. Gaofeng Yuanmiao asks why a single cloud can obscure what shines everywhere; Baichi Xingyuan, Jie Weizhou, and Fusheng Zicong use the phrase as direct answers. Senses.PreferredTarget: At New Year, shake it out before the Chan assembly; such flair truly comes from the master of the house
AlternateTargets: At New Year, display the patched robe to the Chan assembly; that is the style of one who holds the house
SearchAliases: new year shake patched robe before chan assembly
flair from the master of the house
Senses.Note: The inherited verse follows a contrast between last year’s single dark robe and this year’s added patched robe. Shaking it out before the assembly presents this small gain as wealth and “household style.” Wanru and Faxi challenge the show of poverty and wealth; Baichi reverses its claimed riches; Chaozong shakes his own robe in reply; Xingkong seeks a way beyond the division; Pufu warns against boasting of family property. The records assign the wealthy-robe words to Zhenjing or Dongshan Wen; their identity is not settled by their shared wording. Pufu’s quote closes before he speaks the headword in his own voice.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 坐次，乾問云：『居此深山窮谷，有何意思？』綠云：『若無意思，爭引得人到者裏？』乾云：『這裏將謂老兄忘卻。』綠云：『若不忘卻，到不得者裏。』乾云：『領教。』綠云：『又是從頭起。』」師云：「二老若無後語，險些被這裏活埋，至今無有轉身處。何也？既是家裏人，安得灶前坑之深、東廁之高？在這裏也不識，一個東邊瞎衝、一個西邊瞎撞，幾乎將露柱鼻孔撞去半邊。山僧昨承大師遠過，正所謂：『一回相見一回老，能得幾時為弟兄？』自是炊無米飯、點沒油羹，問以詩、答以禮，何必驢唇馬觜至論者也之乎？山僧只合一笑，且道：笑個甚麼？與人恭而有禮？」復云：「又是習氣不除。」元旦，上堂。「元正啟祚，萬物咸新一句作麼生道？」復云：「顛倒顛，新婦騎驢阿家牽，借婆衫子拜婆年。」遂對露柱作女人三拜。復舉：「香嚴云：『去年貧，未是貧；今年貧，始是貧。去年貧，猶有卓錐之地；今年貧，錐也無。』真淨云：『去年富，未是富；今年富，始是富。去年富，唯有一領黑驂布衫；今年添得一條百衲袈娑。』歲朝抖擻呈禪眾，實謂風流出當家。香嚴貧則貧矣，只是不合家醜外傳，逢人嘆氣；真淨富則富矣，又不合賣弄家私，逢人誇豪。若論貧，貧不過永鎮，富，富不過永鎮，富不過永鎮滿堂阿師。那個衣裏無珠？奈彼不能舍用；貧不過永鎮滿堂無位真人，那個身挂寸絲？奈彼無繩自縛。雖然，但貧不嘆貧、富不誇富，仲尼曰：『素富貴，行乎富貴；素貧賤，行乎貧賤。』即如今日山僧同大眾處此堯風舜日，天下晏然，正謂一人有福，兆民賴之，當唱萬年歡，豈非素快活行乎快活？眾中還有知得山僧快活處麼？」撫掌大笑，下座。解制，上堂。舉：「有佛處不得住，無佛處急走過。」師云：「白雲萬里。三千里外，逢人不得錯舉。白雲萬里，恁麼則不去也。白雲萬里摘楊花，摘楊花白雲萬里。永鎮明日設有人來告假，各與草鞋一緉，白雲萬里。何故？不見達觀穎禪師云：『諸方鉤又曲，餌又香，奔走猶如蜂抱王。因聖者裏鉤又直，餌又無，猶如水底捺葫蘆。』永鎮尤不然，鉤又禿，餌又窮，猶如落葉舞狂風。」復云：「白雲萬里。」退院，上堂。「世事悠悠，不如山邱，作麼生是山邱底事？漁翁傍晚曲嵒宿，曉汲青湘然楚竹，煙消日出不見人，款乃一聲山水綠。」遂與大眾拱別，作搖艣勢，云：「款乃，款乃，款乃。」下座。磬山牧亭樸夫拙禪師語錄卷之二住霸陵白鷺渡西汀寺語錄住霸陵白鷺渡西汀

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 歲朝抖擻呈禪眾，實謂風流出當家

Senses.Explanation: A patched robe, shaken out at New Year, becomes a claim about the Chan household’s wealth. Wanru, Baichi, and Faxi each quote the robe verse but question its display of wealth: Baichi finds poverty in it, while Faxi says both sides remain trapped in worldly categories. Chaozong answers by shaking his own robe. Xingkong proposes a joint reading of poor and rich, and Pufu rebukes boasting about the household’s possessions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 結制，太守張護法設齋，請上堂。指法座，云：「千華砌就，百寶堆成，佛佛共坐，祖祖咸陞。今日現於一毫端上，還有與山僧同登者麼？」良久，云：「舉頭天外看，誰是我般人？」卓拄杖，遂陞。拈香祝聖畢，再拈，云：「這瓣香，棒頭花劈，喝下圓成，昔年馥郁黔山，今日澄清昆水。此是第三回拈出，爇向爐中，供養傳臨濟正宗第三十二世先師靈隱文老和尚，用酬法乳之恩。伏願直指佛祖根源，永作人天眼目。」斂衣敷座。維那白椎竟，師云：「若論第一義諦，未陞座時松聲竹籟已道了也，更要畫蛇添足作麼？於中倘有未會者，出眾相見。」問：「孤將入雲陽即不問，忽遇百萬雄兵到來，如何抵敵？」師豎拄杖，云：「單憑一柄吹毛劍。」僧退後，師云：「草賊大敗。」問：「如何是西來大意？」師云：「幾片閒雲飛嶺上。」進云：「如何是涅槃妙心？」師云：「一輪杲日挂天邊。」問：「如來成道二千餘年，和尚成道多少年也？」師云：「忘卻了。」問：「四大五蘊本自空寂，主人公在甚麼處安身立命？」師卓拄杖一下。進云：「可謂不涉語言最親切。」師云：「切忌錯下註腳。」問：「生從何來？」師云：「沒蹤跡處。」進云：「死從何去？」師云：「沒蹤跡處。」進云：「蹤跡既無，甚處住腳？」師云：「沒蹤跡處。」問：「和尚婆心處處，且道為個甚麼？」師豎拂子，云：「為要交代這個。」問：「選佛場開，以何垂示？」師云：「痛棒爇喝。」進云：「恁麼則祖道重興，宗風再振去也。」師云：「有勞讚頌。」乃云：「也大奇，也大奇，將謂拂衣徑過，豈知留錫於茲？選佛場一期結就，龍象眾兩序整齊，金鐘扣處靉靆香雲布座，玉板鳴時繽紛花雨飄墀，可謂法不孤起，仗境而立，道無方所，隨寓即施。」驀豎拄杖，云：「會麼？這裏會得，始知此個消息，如風之在竹、月之在池，不容話會，秪許自知。大覺仙厚著面皮，假一花而拈示；老迦葉萬沒奈何，破雙眉而笑嬉。是以，冤流六十九，遞序到山緇，山緇無別有，單憑杖一枝，魔宮倒挈、虎穴顛提，劈聖解於頃刻、破凡情於片時，致令青山撫掌、綠水揚眉，泥牛踏月吼、木馬驟風嘶，三世能仁憑斯契證，歷代開士即此傳持。正恁麼時，古今同化一句作麼生道？歲歲梅花和雪綻，年年楊柳帶春垂。」結椎，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB447.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Meixi Du of Dongshan. The recurring plum blossoms in snow and spring willows answer a question about continuity within change. Opening a retreat with a meal provided by Governor Zhang, Meixi Fudu raises his staff and says the teaching has no fixed location but works through the circumstances encountered. He recalls the Buddha's flower and Kashyapa's smile, yet says he has nothing separate to offer beyond this staff and the present handling. What sentence expresses ancient and present transforming together? The seasonal pair closes his answer. It is not merely scenery: its recurring freshness caps the address's account of transmission without asserting that the current ceremony repeats every past event unchanged.

Occurrences.Kwic: 元旦，上堂。「冰消雪解，露出乾坤正氣；花發鶯啼，喚回天地公心。萬象森羅，咸霑化育；山河大地，共沐恩榮。人人頌堯天舜日，個個樂義化軒仁。春色平鋪，各秉威靈；一天佳氣，齊承恩力。九有四生，悉具金剛正眼；八難三途，共證無生法忍。若向這裏會得，水流風動，盡談般若；鳥喚猿啼，歌唱陽春。雖然如是，且道林下作麼生話會？」良久，云：「歲歲梅花和雪綻，年年楊柳帶春垂。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB479.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhufengxu of Zhaojue. At New Year, Zhufeng Zhenxu describes melting ice, flowers, orioles and renewed public harmony, joining the season's growth to wishes for ruler and people. If understood here, flowing water, moving wind and animal calls all speak complete discernment. Yet how will those living beneath the trees express it? After a pause he gives the plum-and-willow pair. The familiar annual return becomes his present reply after the expansive blessing. The source does not identify a particular plum tree or willow witnessed that morning, nor make a meteorological promise that every year must have the same snow.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the paired scene of a water-drawing monastic returning to the forest temple and a traveler waiting on the ferrybank sand

Senses.Explanation: The couplet places two ordinary figures in transit: the water-drawing monastic returns to a forest temple while a traveler waits for a boat on the ferrybank sand. Fodeng Shouxun’s verse follows an appraisal of Daowu’s answer about a wildfire; Hunyuan Mi’s case-verse sets the same waterside couplet among river, sail, and night-sky images.

Senses.Explanation: Thread coming, line going names a close back-and-forth movement, using the joined motion of thread and sewing line. Dahui Zonggao caps an encounter with the line; Yuanwu Keqin compares Danxia and Layman Pang's exchange to it, saying it is half closing and half opening; Xingjiao Poyun uses it of stitching where wind cannot pass. These cases retain the textile image across comment and direct address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 日轉光輝師云一道舊行路高下自分明進云只如大顛叩齒韓文公直下知歸黃檗安名裴相國便知落處未審和尚今日與知縣朝議相見有何指示師云兩眼對兩眼進云莫便是指示也無師云一任鑽龜打瓦僧禮拜。師乃云問得亦好不問更親何故聲前一路千聖不傳學者勞形如猿捉影可中有箇英靈漢恁麼不恁麼聊聞舉著剔起便行猶在葛藤窠裏直得內無所證外無所修似地擎山如石含玉亦未是衲僧放身命處敢問法筵大眾作麼生是衲僧放身命處若也知得塵塵念念皆無空闕折旋俯仰盡在其

Senses.Explanation: Before sound marks the point at which a Chan exchange is tested before an utterance has become an audible phrase. Masters ask for a “phrase before sound,” say it is already exposed, or warn that even discerning it can remain incomplete. The expression therefore does not name silent time in general: it sets speech against what the encounter demands before speech can be leaned on.

OwnerReview.Scope: one-pass semantic, source-attribution, and construction review

Senses.PreferredTarget: the phrase before sound
Senses.Note: The phrase before sound is a test of whether a speaker can answer before turning the answer into another verbal object. Foguo, Miyun, Tianyin, Feiyin, and Xuzhou give distinct current hall applications; a monk offers it to Sanshan, who refuses a ready answer. The phrase remains one Chan prompt despite these different replies.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase before sound is said not to be handed down even by a thousand sages, yet masters make that very claim the opening of a public test rather than a reason to remain mute. An unnamed monk asks Jinian Jingxian what the non-transmission means, and Jinian answers, ‘a Persian chews icy iron.’ Tianyin Yuanxiu says students who chase it through words labor like an ape grasping at a reflection, while Yuanwu Keqin uses the line to open a Blue Cliff case and immediately challenges the assembly to present it. The saying denies inherited verbal possession while functioning audibly as question, pointer, and answer-demand. That tension is the corpus's observable use; the entry does not turn ‘before sound’ into an outside metaphysical claim.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 累它補處慈尊，至今坐在𡏖𡒁堆頭。逕山亦於一時中成就五百個衲子，證自在神通。且道說甚麼法？良久，云：適逢中夏，叢林暑假。上堂，舉：僧問雲門：秋初夏末，前程忽有人問，將何祗對？門云：大眾退後。僧云：有甚麼過？門云：還我九十日飯錢來。師頌云：飯錢還未了，世路又忩忩。萬里八九月，一身西北風。冬至，上堂。魯史書雲，漢宮添線，五湖龍象交參，第一義諦作麼舉？履茲佳旦，恭惟首座大眾，各各尊侯，動止多福。上堂：向上一路，何處尋討？飢來喫飯，寒來著襖。金粟通身是病，文殊一見便好。大眾！天寒不宜久立，各自歸堂向火。上堂，舉：僧問歸宗：如何是佛？宗云：我與汝說，汝還信得及麼？僧云：和尚誠言，焉敢不信？宗云：只汝便是。僧云：如何保任？宗云：一翳在眼，空華亂墜。師拈云：藕絲竅裏跨鵾鵬，蟭螟眼中放夜市。上堂，舉溈山問雲巖云：如何是藥山大人相？雲巖云：涅槃後有。溈山云：如何是涅槃後有？巖云：水洒不著。巖却問溈山云：如何是百丈大人相？溈山云：巍巍堂堂，煒煒煌煌。聲前非聲，色後非色。蚊子上鐵牛，無你下觜處。師頌云：三十二相，八十種好。水灑不著，切忌落草。蚊子上鐵牛，未免成懊惱。休懊惱，天上人間何處討？遇五，示眾。鉏畬種粟，㘽田博飯，衲僧家本分上事。考鐘伐鼓，普請上堂，視堂戶不啻牢禁，又何如哉？諸禪德，未明心地印，滴水也難消。上堂：一夏九十日，龍門無宿客。三處度夏七佛師，愁殺摩訶老迦葉。以拂子擊禪床一下：野色更無山隔斷，天光直與水相通。解制，小參。翠巖一夏與兄弟東語西話，落盡眉毛，不覺精神十倍。臨濟遭黃檗打趂，中途疑著此事，再回終夏，換却多少鶻眼鷹睛。雲門道：和尚子莫妄想，天是天，地是地，山是山，水是水，僧是僧，俗是俗。良久，云：與我拈按山來，木人拍板雲中立，石女吹笙水上行。僧便問：學人見山是山、見水是水時如何？門云：三門為什麼騎佛殿從者裏過？西風一陣來，落葉兩三片。僧云：與麼則不妄想也。門云：還我話頭來，山頭石虎吼聲乾，海底驪龍拗角折。遂以主丈畫一畫，喝一喝。除夜，小參。無邊剎境，自它不隔於毫端；十世古今，始終不離於當念。山僧與諸人共汎一隻無底鐵舡，釋迦千百億化身坐舡頭、文殊堂裏萬菩薩坐舡尾，打鹽官鼓、唱德山歌，然後穿過東弗于逮也住千百億劫、北󳬂單越也住千百億劫、西瞿耶尼也住千百億劫、南贍部洲也住千百

Senses.Explanation: The paired sensory objects of ear and eye: sound (聲) and visible form or color (色). Chan records do more than repeat the pair abstractly. Yongjia's exchange explicitly assigns them to the faculties — 'when eyes and ears meet sound and form' (眼耳緣聲色時) — and asks what is the substance of sound and form. Dahui makes the pair demonstrable during a public address: he raises the whisk and says, 'this is form,' strikes the Chan seat and says, 'this is sound' (這箇是色／這箇是聲). Another record gives ordinary audible examples: wind in pine trees, frogs, and crows are all sound, while saying that what one discriminates is sound and form. The corpus also predicates 'pass through all sound and form without obstruction' (透一切聲色，無有滯礙) and draws its own distinction between function 'together with sound and form' and 'the affairs of sound and form' (用同聲色而不是聲色之事). The Zen deviation is this repeated use as a named field of public testing and concrete demonstration; the graphs still denote what is heard and seen.

Senses.PreferredTarget: sensual attractions and entertainments
Senses.Note: The phrase 'cast off sensual attractions' (擯去聲色) occurs in nine texts, chiefly recensions of the same Zhao Bian biography; 'indulge in sensual attractions' (耽聲色) supplies a structurally independent witness. No distinctively Chan lexical bend was found for this ordinary sense. Across the collected corpus the expression has 2545 exact occurrences in 334 distinct works.

Senses.Explanation: A distinct ordinary referent in biographical and admonitory prose: worldly sensual attractions or entertainments, commonly coordinated with wealth, status, and profit. Zhao Bian's biography says that after forty he 'cast off sensual attractions' (擯去聲色) and turned his attention to the records of the school. Another record warns against simultaneously pursuing achievement, receiving wealth and honor, 'indulging in sensual attractions' (耽聲色), and attending to worldly affairs. This is not the eye-and-ear field concretely demonstrated by a whisk and struck seat, so it remains a separate sense.

Senses.Explanation: The two outward signs in the fixed phrase 'without changing voice or expression' (不動聲色): voice or tone (聲) and facial look or demeanor (色). A record praises Huanglong's forty years presiding over a community as 'holding the seat of the community without changing voice or expression' (坐鎮道場，不動聲色); a public interview likewise asks whether something can be discerned 'without changing voice or expression.' This idiomatic human demeanor is a different referent from sounds and visible objects in the sensory field.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Form is emptiness; emptiness is form
AlternateTargets: Form itself is empty; emptiness itself is form
Senses.Note: The paired Heart Sutra line says the relation of form and emptiness works in both directions. Zhuanyu explains how it guides seeing form; Hanyue uses it to discuss the aggregates; Pu’an places it beside Mazu’s teaching on mind and form; another recorded teacher presents it as a point where scripture and Chan meet. These teachers use the familiar words to explain or test understanding in their own settings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃作證道歌一首，發明禪宗教外別傳之道，揀去權淺之病，皆自證心流出。其摧邪顯正，如出匣鏌鋣，光芒燭天，勢不可犯。自有宗門以來，僅一見之。因思古今得道者眾，要如大海水、阿修羅，以及魚龍蝦蠏，恣其所飲，各滿其量而已。若永嘉可謂掀翻大海，傾竭無餘，真禪關之樞要，別傳之顯訣。傳布西天，共美之曰證道經，不誣也。石頭希遷禪師參同契石頭希遷禪師參同契竺土大仙心，東西密相付。人根有利鈍，道無南北祖。靈源明皎潔，枝派暗流注。執事元是迷，契理亦非悟。門門一切境，迴互不迴互。迴而更相涉，不爾依位住。色本殊質象，聲元異樂苦。暗合上中言，明明清濁句。四大性自復，如子得其母。火熱風動搖，水濕地堅固。眼色耳音聲，鼻香舌鹹醋。然依一一法，依根葉分布。本末須歸宗，尊卑用其語。當明中有暗，勿以暗相遇。當暗中有明，勿以明相覩。明暗各相對，比如前後步。萬物自有功，當言用及處。事存函盖合，理應箭鋒拄。承言須會宗，勿自立規矩。觸目不會道，運足焉知路。進步非近遠，迷隔山河固。謹白參玄人，光陰莫虗度。論曰：石頭和尚因讀肇論，會萬物為己之言，遂悟聖人無己，靡所不己。又夢與六祖同乘靈智，遊於性海，此參同契所由作。句句皆法
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1442.xml). Drafts from Chan Master Weilin’s Traveling Hermitage. Weilin Daopei's collected drafts reproduce the poem under a heading naming Shitou Xiqian, followed by Weilin's own discussion. Before this pair, the poem says that the fields encountered through the senses both interact and keep their own places. It then distinguishes forms in substance and shape and sounds as pleasant or painful, moves through darkness and clarity, and compares the four elements returning to their own natures to a child finding its mother. The following lines name heat, movement, moisture and solidity, then eyes and forms, ears and sounds, nose and scent, and tongue and tastes. The pair keeps these differences audible and visible within the poem's discussion of interaction and distinct position. This is Shitou's attributed poem being transmitted, not a newly spoken claim by Weilin; its placement in a master-authored collection alone does not establish historical composition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 流注。執事元是迷，契理亦非悟。靈源，心也，本不落名言，因明而見其皎潔。枝派，事也，本無有實體，因暗而見其流注。枝派流注，是謂執事，認妄為真，固是迷矣。靈源皎潔，是謂契理，有理可契，豈為真悟乎？此言明之與暗，總妄明之顯晦，學者不可依之以自惑也。門門一切境，回互不回互，回而更相涉，不爾依位住。門，根也。境，塵也。諸根境有回互不回互二義。言回互者，謂諸根境互相涉入，如帝網珠也。不回互者，謂諸根境各住本位，未嘗混雜也。雖互相涉入，而實各住本位。雖各住本位，而實互相涉入。此非意識之境。色本殊質象，聲元異樂苦。暗合上中言，明明清濁句。四大性自復，如子得其母。此明色聲諸法，熾然殊異，暗則上中莫辨，明則清濁攸分，此皆滯於迹而不能反於性也。若反於性，豈有明暗之可言哉。正如子得其母，天然妙契，而知與不知，俱不足言矣。火熱風動搖，水濕地堅固，眼色耳音聲，鼻香舌鹹醋。然於一一法，依根葉分布，本末須歸宗，尊卑用其語。諸法雖殊，總根於心。心，本也；諸法，末也。然必有宗焉。宗者，諸佛之秘要，列祖之玄旨。不達此宗，則本末俱妄；能達此宗，則本末俱真。此宗既得，由是出一言，行一令，無非毗盧之正印，孰能不
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian. Yongjue Yuanxian quotes the pair while explaining the attributed Shitou poem. In the preceding gloss, he says the sensory faculties and their objects can enter into one another while each remains in its own position, without confusion. After quoting the form-and-sound lines with the darkness, clarity and child-and-mother lines, he says that forms and sounds are vividly different: darkness prevents certain distinctions, while light separates clear from turbid. Yet he calls reliance on either darkness or light remaining with traces instead of returning to nature. If one returns to nature, he asks, how can darkness or light still be spoken of? Like a child finding its mother, the accord is natural, and neither knowing nor not knowing adequately states it. Thus Yongjue does not erase the listed differences; his present interpretation challenges taking their illuminated or obscured appearances as the end of the matter. The exact pair remains the quoted poem's voice, and the ensuing explanation is Yongjue's own.

Occurrences.Kwic: 示然藏主德然上人！你參我老石屋和尚指示道：「但於十二時中放下全身，坐斷主人公，不起第二念。」可謂是的的從祖佛相傳，不可傳、不可授、不可說底意旨矣。只如你全身放得下麼？一箇臭皮袋子，饑時要粥飯吃，不吃則肚饑過不得，如何全身放下？一法如是，萬法亦然；自己如是，眾人亦然；佛祖聖賢如是，凡夫亦然；一切眾生亦然。正放下時，身在甚麼處？放不下時，你在甚麼處？放得下不曾放下，放不下何用放下？人境俱空，凡聖俱泯，又何處現釋迦老子與石屋和尚？又向何處參父母未生前面目？又向何處求無明法語？又向何處入彌勒樓閣？會得赤肉團上有一箇無位真人，能分許多位次。眼須觀色，不為色所迷；耳須聽聲，不為聲所惑。世間色見聲求，是行邪道。若行見聞覺知，是則見聞覺知，非求法也。求底是心，見聞覺知是？心佛是？不是心、不是佛、不是物，一拳打碎虛空骨，森羅萬象眼睛開，鼻孔何妨高突兀？然藏主！你如今既為頭首，以字不成、八字不是，適來對眾喝我一喝，三十年後有人勘你在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB273.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Qianyan. In instruction to librarian Deran, Qianyan Yuanzhang tests the command to put down the whole body: hunger still requires food, so where is the body when one puts it down or cannot? Eyes must see forms without being misled, and ears hear sounds without being confused. He then says seeking through form and sound follows a mistaken path, distinguishing sensory knowing from seeking the teaching. The headword is his present scriptural formulation inside that examination. It does not require blindness or deafness; his final reminder that Deran's public shout may be tested thirty years later also blocks treating a lively gesture as sufficient proof.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛涅槃，上堂。「色見聲求，是行邪道。那堪摩胸告眾，要人觀紫磨金色之身。是正道？是邪道？咄哉瞿曇！郎當不少，即今不屬有無。大眾還見麼？晴光轉綠蘋，淑氣催黃鳥。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB388.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yikui of Shending. At the commemoration of the Buddha's final release, Yikui Yuankui begins with seeking through form and sound as a mistaken path. Why then, he asks, does the Buddha touch his chest and tell everyone to look at the golden body: is this the right path or a wrong one? He rebukes Gautama's complications, then says the present is not confined to being and nonbeing. Can the assembly see? Clear light on green water plants and mild air urging yellow birds close the address. The formula is Yikui's current critical opening, deliberately brought into tension with the bodily farewell, rather than a straightforward prohibition on looking.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂提拄杖卓一下乃顧視曰拄杖子拄杖子你無住持干懷又無病痛苦惱如此黑瘦何也拈拄杖呵呵大笑曰是何言也若色見聲求是行邪道昔臨濟德山由之發明見諦後來明眼尊宿由之接物度人豈不見黃蘗普請次蘗謂臨濟曰我最得者拄杖氣力臨濟近前奪下拄杖推倒黃蘗黃蘗遂曰扶起我來扶起我來時有一僧近前扶起曰和尚爭容得者風顛漢恁地無禮蘗却打其僧數下臨濟乃曰蒼天蒼天大眾當時拄杖子如今却在龍門手裏乃提起召大眾曰還有臨濟手叚底麼出來出來龍門却是放得下遂拋下拄杖放身便倒曰有扶得者出來良久曰既無臨濟之人又無扶起之者龍門自起自倒有甚用處歸堂去下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (C/C077/C077n1710.xml). Recorded Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters. Foyan Qingyuan raises his staff, asks why it is so thin and dark despite having neither abbot's concerns nor illness, then laughs at his own words. If seeking through form and sound is a mistaken path, he asks, how did earlier teachers realize through such means and use them to help people? He raises Huangbo and Linji's staff struggle, then repeats its challenge: lifting and dropping his own staff, he falls down and asks who can lift him. With no response, he says he gets up and falls by himself and sends the assembly away. The headword is a premise put under pressure by the enacted exchange, not a detached rejection of visible and audible teaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第十則蓮華不住舉：蓮華庵主拈拄杖示眾云：古人到這裏，為什麼不肯住？眾無語。自代云：為他途路不得力。復云：畢竟如何？又自云：楖𣗖橫擔不顧人，直入千峯萬峰去。天童拈云：負入不負出，本色住山人。思大吞盡諸佛，普眼不見普賢。且道病在什麼處？驀拈拄杖卓一下，云：官不容針，私通車馬。師云：江州廬山蓮華峰祥庵主，嗣奉先深禪師，雲門嫡孫，知見甚高，氣壓諸方，履踐分明，非常情所測。師臨終上堂，舉拄杖問眾曰：汝道古佛到這裏，為什麼不肯住？萬松道：生怕枯樁繫鈍驢。石室行者善道禪師，時遭沙汰，常以拄杖示眾曰：過去諸佛也恁麼，未來諸佛也恁麼，現在諸佛也恁麼。萬松道：歷代祖師不恁麼。不見道：丈夫自有沖天志，不向如來行處行。雪峰一日僧堂前拈拄杖示眾云：這箇祗為中下根人。時有僧出問云：忽遇上上人來時如何？峰拈拄杖便去。雲門云：我即不似雪峯打破狼藉。僧問：未審和尚如何？雲門便打。萬松道：狼藉不少。駙馬都尉李文和公，公主貴降，命三大宗師同日陞座，末後葉縣橫拄杖就膝上抝作兩截，便下座。公曰：老作家手段終別。縣云：都尉也不得無過。庵主舉此話示眾：臨終散場，大作佛事。眾竟無語。一曲離騷歸去後，汨羅江上獨醒人。自代云：為他途路不得力。萬松恁麼舉，諸人恁麼聽，若無得力處，彼各圖箇什麼？却道途路不得力。葢色見聲求，是行邪道；忘聲泯色，是斷滅相。途路之樂，終不到家。燈錄廣本更有一句復問：作麼生得力去？萬松道：臨行之際，撒手還家，指出路頭，還須拄杖。燈錄復有橫拄杖於肩上曰：楖𣗖橫擔不顧人，却入千峰萬峰去。天童作直入，各有理在。嚴陽尊者路逢一僧，拈拄杖云：是什麼？僧云：不識。嚴云：拄杖一條也不識。嚴復以拄杖地上劄一下云：還識麼？僧云：不識。嚴云：土窩箇也不識。嚴復拈拄杖擔云：會麼？僧云：不會。嚴云：楖𣗖橫擔不顧人，直入千峯萬峰去。便見蓮峰末後轉身吐氣，羅籠不住，呼喚不回。紅塵擾擾道常在，何況碧山深更深。天童拈道：負入不負出，本色住山人。祗有受璧心，而無割城意。羅什道：有非真要，時復蹔游。空為理宗，以為常宅。華嚴普眼入百千三昧，終不見普賢。亦猶大通智勝佛，十劫坐道場，竟不成佛道。梁誌公遣僧傳語南岳思大和尚云：何不下山教化眾生，向山頭目視雲漢作麼？思大云：三世諸佛被我一口吞盡，何處更有眾生可度？天童密罰，却道：病在甚麼處？不見道：莫守寒巖異草青，坐著白雲宗不妙。任是深山更深處，也應無處避征徭。風穴拈云：若立一塵，家國興盛。故天童拈起拄杖卓一下云：官不容針，私通車馬。古人以向上路為本分事，以建化門頭曲為今時。慈覺道：有為雖偽，棄之則功行不成；無為雖真，趣之則聖果難尅。天童經事多矣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1307.xml). Elder Wansong’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Master Tiantong Jue’s Picking Up Ancient Cases: Record of Requests for Instruction. Wansong Xingxiu comments on the Lotus Peak hermit's question about why earlier Buddhas would not remain here and his answer that the road offers no effective support. After comparing several staff encounters, Wansong asks why teaching and listening would matter if they offered no help at all. He sets seeking through forms and sounds as a mistaken path beside erasing sound and form as an image of annihilation: pleasure along the road still does not reach home. Yet he adds that pointing out the road requires the staff. The headword belongs to this balanced present commentary, limiting sensory attachment without granting an escape into blank suppression.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有異比丘以金剛經寫成釋迦佛像，高不五寸，廣則半之，可視不可讀，為作贊曰：三十二相，金剛法寶。色見聲求，是行邪道。應無所住，而生其心。夢幻露電，功德之林。縱橫倒植，珠明玉潤。毫端發揮，攝入方寸。如明鏡中，而現色像。善哉佛子，顯此智藏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao’an Qingyu. Liao'an Qingyu writes a praise for a monk who has copied the Diamond Scripture into a tiny image of Shakyamuni, visible but too small to read. The poem names the Buddha's marks and the scriptural treasure, then warns that seeking through form and sound is a mistaken path. It continues with non-abiding mind and dream, illusion, dew and lightning, finally praising the image's bright, mirror-like manifestation and the monk's wisdom. The headword is actively woven into Liao'an's praise of a visible artifact. Its juxtaposition with that praise matters: the poem does not simply declare the image useless or claim that its appearance alone conveys realization.

Senses.PreferredTarget: patch-robed monk
Senses.Note: The records use the same human-role noun individually, collectively, and possessively. Yuanwu calls raising one and understanding three “ordinary tea and rice for the household of patch-robed monks” (衲僧家尋常茶飯), and elsewhere calls activity that ferries beings “the patch-robed monk's own affair” (衲僧家本分事). Eye, gate, conduct, air, household, own portion, and handle compounds do not denote a second kind of monk. Compare monk (僧), master or preceptor (和尚), this old monk (老僧), the household of patch-robed monks (衲僧家), and patched robe (衲衣).

Senses.Explanation: A patch-robed monk is the Chan participant marked by the patched robe and repeatedly addressed, questioned, and appraised in public encounters. The robe-word becomes a public standard in compounds asking after the patch-robed monk's eye, conduct, own affair, house, and manner. Asked “what is a patch-robed monk?” (如何是衲僧), one reviewed exchange answers, “investigating, seeking, and visiting the Way” (參尋訪道). Another exchange asks for “the patch-robed monk's own affair” (衲僧分上事) and answers, “when you want to walk, walk; when you want to sit, sit” (要行即行，要坐即坐). The corpus also asks directly about “the patch-robed monk's eye” (衲僧眼) and “the patch-robed monk's place of conduct” (衲僧行履處). It speaks institutionally of what can be used “under the patch-robed monk's gate” (衲僧門下), and appraises an assembly as lacking anyone with “the air of a patch-robed monk” (衲僧氣息). The Chan deviation lies in this public standard: the robe-word names the person expected to answer within the encounter record, while the compounds test that person's eye, conduct, handle, own affair, and house. These are attested compound uses, not claims about an inner state.

The Chan monk's vital handle is the essential point or effective grasp at issue in a teaching turn, rather than a piece of monastic equipment. Cremating the bones of Dawang, Tianyin Yuanxiu plays on the deceased's name: seeing through delusion, understand the true basis and know the four elements are empty. Today, he says, he communicates the monk's vital matter. He throws the torch and tells them to look: let the white bones be burned, without moving an eyebrow. Senses.Explanation: A patch-robed monk’s proper business is what remains when accomplishment, verbal display, and borrowed devices are set aside. Masters ask for it directly, deny that spectacular feats amount to it, and answer the question with words or blows that must themselves be met in the interview. Yuanwu Keqin says even extraordinary accomplishments are not yet the patch-robed monk’s proper business, then asks for a statement outside accomplishment. Tianyin Yuanxiu says that even overwhelming shouts and blows are not it, asks what it is, and answers with a verse whose standing peaks do not turn the label into a generic achievement. Poshan Haiming calls ordinary travel and attendance the patch-robed monk’s proper business, but immediately says that this still is not the ancestral visitor’s meaning. Xueqiao Yuanxin answers the direct question with repeated blows. Dahui Zonggao likewise raises the question after listing feats and refers the hearer to the two appointed seats.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1296.xml). Compilation of the School Gate’s “Raising Old Cases”. A Chan practitioner's 'eye' here is tested discernment, not simply the physical ability to see. Dahui Zonggao examines the story of a demon king who will form the resolve to awaken only after all beings have become Buddhas and even their name has disappeared. He criticizes earlier answers, including a contrast of open-eyed light and closed-eyed darkness, then proposes saying, 'I almost mistakenly called you a demon king.' He says this response has two vulnerable openings: anyone who detects them may be granted the practitioner's eye. The phrase names the capacity to examine even the teacher's proposed answer, not automatic assent to it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB287.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zixianjue. Speaking from the head seat at Tiantong, Zixian Jue describes the mountain monastery as the lion's cave and a home of the teaching, with Buddha-and-ancestor activity disclosed everywhere and the practitioner's eye opened in every mote. He immediately qualifies this: without clarity about one's own fundamental matter, all remains vague and approximate, especially amid the fierce teachers evoked as tigers and dragons. Raising his whisk, he ends with streams returning to the sea and mountains looking toward their source. The eye must become one's own effective recognition; impressive surroundings alone do not supply it.

Senses.Explanation: A Chan practitioner's 'eye' here is tested discernment, not simply the physical ability to see. Dahui Zonggao examines the story of a demon king who will form the resolve to awaken only after all beings have become Buddhas and even their name has disappeared. He criticizes earlier answers, including a contrast of open-eyed light and closed-eyed darkness, then proposes saying, 'I almost mistakenly called you a demon king.' He says this response has two vulnerable openings: anyone who detects them may be granted the practitioner's eye. The phrase names the capacity to examine even the teacher's proposed answer, not automatic assent to it. An unnamed monk asks Wufeng Ruxue directly what the practitioner's eye is. Wufeng replies that the questioner cannot be deceived even a little. But when the monk hesitates, Wufeng says he is not someone from inside the house after all. The second response tests the apparently confident first one; the passage does not simply award the monk unfailing discernment because he asked about it. At winter solstice, Baichi Xingyuan says the accumulated yin has been stripped away and one yang returns, then joins the practitioner's upright eye to walking freely throughout the world. He shouts and descends. The seasonal reversal supplies the compact address's occasion, while the eye names the orientation needed for that freedom. The turn gives no anatomical description or method of reading the future from the calendar. An unnamed monk asks Tui'an Duanyu Zhenzhi what the practitioner's eye is and receives 'Blind.' Asked for the meaning, the teacher again says 'Blind.' The repeated refusal obstructs an expectation that this eye must be an enhanced seeing faculty with an available explanation. The record does not resolve the paradox into a doctrine that physical blindness itself constitutes realization. Speaking from the head seat at Tiantong, Zixian Jue describes the mountain monastery as the lion's cave and a home of the teaching, with Buddha-and-ancestor activity disclosed everywhere and the practitioner's eye opened in every mote. He immediately qualifies this: without clarity about one's own fundamental matter, all remains vague and approximate, especially amid the fierce teachers evoked as tigers and dragons. Raising his whisk, he ends with streams returning to the sea and mountains looking toward their source. The eye must become one's own effective recognition; impressive surroundings alone do not supply it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禮休去。乃無端却謂應當如是，隨風倒舵，豈是丈夫？天界盛云：世尊言中有響，阿難句裏藏鋒，并須喫棒有分。為什麼聻？人天師表，不合用以機械。蓮柎䇿云：阿難不唧𠺕，當時見道是吾弟子，何不便禮三拜，管教者黃面老子置身無地。世尊於自恣日，因文殊三處過夏，迦葉欲白椎擯出。纔拈椎，乃見百千萬億文殊。迦葉盡其神力，椎不能舉。世尊遂問迦葉：汝擬擯那個文殊？迦葉無對。昭覺勤云：可惜放過當時，待釋迦老子道汝擬擯那個文殊，便與一椎，看他作何合殺？雲居元云：一家有事百家忙。天童覺云：金色頭陀，有心無膽，當時盡令而行，莫道百千萬億文殊，祇者黃面瞿曇也與擯出，不唯壁立真風，亦令後人知我衲僧門下著你閒佛閒祖不得。保寧茂云：大小迦葉有頭無尾，畢竟如何？西天令嚴。久立，珍重。高峰妙云：文殊知底，迦葉不知；迦葉知底，文殊不知。彼彼不知則且置，百千萬億文殊，畢竟那個是真文殊？天寧琦云：迦葉太不丈夫，莫道百千萬億文殊，便是百千萬億世尊，也下一椎擯出，始見作家。不見道：棒下無生忍，臨機不見師。龍池傳云：我若作迦葉，把黃面老子先須擯却。何故？來說是非者，便是是非人。鼓山賢云：文殊雖得便宜，怎奈轉增醜態。當時何不默受擯去，教他迦葉三十年摸索不著。寶壽新云：文殊行處，迦葉不知；迦葉做處，文殊不識。唯黃面老子，有顯有密，有權有實。怎見得聻？咬牙封雍齒，滴淚斬丁公。

Senses.Explanation: The wearer of patched monastic robes: a patch-robed monk or monk in patched robes. The term is attested and names monks whom Chan teachers address, question, appraise, and describe through their clothing, livelihood, daily activity, and house style. Pin Jixiang gives a direct naming formula: 'Each wears a hat and waist-pack and is named a patch-robed monk; name and reality should match' (箇箇都是頂笠腰包，名為衲子，要當名實相稱). Nanquan Puyuan says, 'Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish; patch-robed monks are hard to fool' (龍蛇易辨衲子難謾). Yushan Shangsi calls an astute patch-robed monk difficult to find (伶俐衲子難得), while Jingqing Daofu twice praises Fengxue Yanzhao as 'a fine patch-robed monk' (衲子俊哉). Zhufeng Zhenxu says, 'The patch-robed monk's eyebrows leap' (衲子眉毛𨁝跳), in an end-of-retreat hall verse. Minshu names a snow hat and cloud gourd as 'the patch-robed monk's livelihood' (雪笠雲瓢，為衲子之活計). Haizhuang Azi Jinwu says that the patch-robed monk's daily activity already has a great treasury of light and requires being such a person. Hansong Zhicao contrasts 'keeping to poverty and quiet, the patch-robed monk's house style' with 'pursuing warmth and bustle, the ordinary person's livelihood' (固窮守寂，衲子家風；附熱趨喧，常人活計). Asked directly, 'What is a patch-robed monk?' (如何是衲子), Shanhui answers, 'Bare-bodied atop Mount Sumeru; do not go toward the northern continent' (赤身須彌頂，莫向越單行). Zen bends a clothing label into an institutional and interpersonal name for the monks addressed and tested in the teaching community; it does not make praise, clothing, or house style into separate person-senses.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The book title and poem heading 送彼岸禪人住山 identify Poshan as the author of the exact headword-bearing verse.

Senses.Explanation: To pull the patchwork quilt over one’s head is to withdraw completely from claims, schemes, and public business. Chan masters use monastic bedding as an image of radical non-involvement: ten thousand matters stop, even claims to understand are set aside. Yunfeng joins the covered head to letting all matters rest; Yuanwu quotes the same line when asking how to raise the guestless-hostless saying at the hearth; Hongjue includes it among proposed escapes from mental binding and rejects treating it as an automatic solution; and Poshan’s farewell verse sends a practitioner into the mountains with the quilt over his head even if a thousand Buddhas appear.

Senses.Explanation: A monk covers his head with his quilt and lets all affairs rest, saying that even he does not understand. Chaozong gives the line after asking what freedom is. Tian’an ends a stern address with it. Chuiwan uses it after asking what remains beyond a posed pair of figures, and Hanxiu gives it in response to a winter-solstice question.

Senses.Explanation: To cover heaven and encompass earth is to have complete spatial reach. Shending Yin applies it to one sentence, Zhenjing Kewen pairs it with extending through past and present, and Shiqi Tongyun uses it for the reach of directly grasping the matter. The two coordinated verbs retain their literal directions while functioning as one totalizing expression.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。如是我聞，遲日江山麗，春風花草香。諸佛出世，眼瞎耳聾。達磨西來，眼瞎耳聾。衲僧成團成塊，眼瞎耳聾。若是箇漢，向黑荳未生已前信受奉行去，三十年後方知。且道知箇什麼眼瞎耳聾？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1371.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Jieshi Zhipeng. Jieshi Zhipeng begins an address with the scriptural opening 'Thus have I heard,' then gives the long spring days, beautiful rivers and mountains, and fragrant flowers and grasses in the spring wind. He abruptly calls the appearance of Buddhas, Bodhidharma's arrival and the assembled monks blind and deaf. A capable person is to receive and enact it before the black beans have grown, understanding only thirty years later; he then asks what this blindness and deafness is. The sensory clarity of the opening is placed against the challenge of actually hearing and seeing. His deliberately unsettling language is not a clinical description of the listeners, and the address leaves its final question open.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛涅槃，上堂。記得世尊涅槃日，普告大眾云：謂吾滅度，非吾弟子；謂吾不滅度，亦非吾弟子。師云：滅度、不滅度既總不是，畢竟合作麼生？諸人還見釋迦老子麼？其或未然，却聽山僧分明為汝指出：遲日江山麗，春風花草香。泥融飛鷰子，沙暖睡鴛鴦。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1382.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuzhun Shifan. On the commemoration of the Buddha's final release, Wuzhun Shifan raises a saying that neither declaring the Buddha extinct nor declaring him not extinct makes one his disciple. If both are wrong, what is to be done? Can the listeners see Shakyamuni? Wuzhun says he will point him out clearly, then gives the spring-day pair and continues with swallows flying over softened mud and paired birds sleeping on warm sand. The headword is Wuzhun's present answer through a fully pictured scene, not an assertion that one can settle the Buddha's condition by choosing one verbal alternative. The continuation supplies the concrete birds, mud and sand that a bare reference to 'spring' would miss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：至化無方，至德有光。遲日江山麗，春風花草香。玉壺影裡劫春長，乾坤獨露堂堂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1397.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xueyan Zuqin. Xueyan Zuqin opens his short address with transforming influence that has no fixed direction and virtue that shines. He gives the beautiful spring landscape and fragrant flowers and grass, then adds long spring within the image of a jade vessel and the world standing fully revealed. The phrase is not embedded in a question-and-answer exchange here. Its visible, scented spring scene gives body to the opening praise, while the final images remain compressed. The source does not provide a separate technical explanation of the jade vessel or a prescribed exercise for reproducing the scene.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三月三大聖生日，上堂。舉泗州大聖國師昔日有問云：住在何國？答曰：何國。又問云：何姓？答曰：姓何。拈云：東涌西沒，七縱八橫，則不無大聖，其奈醜惡俱露。茲遇誕辰，拈拄杖云：拄杖子未免應時應節下箇注脚。卓一下云：遲日江山麗，春風花草香。泥融飛燕子，沙暖睡鴛鴦。擲拄杖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1404.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wu’an Puning. On the birthday of the Sizhou saint, Wu'an Puning raises the exchange in which the saint repeats the questioner's 'what' wording in answers about country and surname. Wu'an grants its freedom of movement but says its ugliness is also exposed. For the present anniversary, he raises his staff, calls it a comment appropriate to the occasion, strikes it and gives the spring-day pair followed by swallows over soft mud and paired birds on warm sand. He then throws down the staff. The headword belongs to Wu'an's current seasonal cap, distinct from the saint's quoted answers and from an explanatory resolution of their wordplay.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB485.xml). Pumen Xian asks in his own sermon whether one fixes on magpie and crow calls and sensory awareness, then warns that attachment to them misses the point.

Senses.Explanation: Magpie chatter and crow calls become ordinary sound through which the point can be seen or missed. Baichi Xingyuan includes the sounds in a birthday sermon on unity with daily life; Pumen Xian uses them to question attachment to sensory awareness.
